claims.title: saveReviewState always increments even for non-review callers
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**saveReviewState always increments even for non-review callers**

`saveReviewState` now unconditionally increments `reviewCount` on every call, including the call in `parsePriorReview`'s cold-start recovery path (state.reviewCount is set to 0 there) and any other place that persists state without it representing an actual new review being posted. If saveReviewState is ever called more than once for the same logical review (e.g. retried on a transient KV failure, or from a different call site added later), the count will over-increment. Consider making the increment explicit at the call site (i.e., have callers pass the already-incremented value) rather than baking a side-effecting mutation into the generic save function, since `saveReviewState`'s name/signature doesn't signal that it mutates the passed-in state's count.

claims.title: metadata regex extraction could match unintended earlier occurrences
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**metadata regex extraction could match unintended earlier occurrences**

`extract()` uses `body.match(new RegExp(...))` without the global flag, so it returns the first match. If a review body ever contains a nested/quoted example of the metadata syntax (e.g., in a code block showing sample output, or in a finding's `evidence`/`body` text that quotes another review's metadata), `parseReviewMetadata` could pick up the wrong value. This is a minor robustness concern given metadata blocks are appended at the end and unlikely to be duplicated, but the function has no other named field, and could be tightened by anchoring to line start and using a shared join point.

claims.title: formatFindings 3-column output breaks the cold-KV recovery row parser
claims.text:
🟠 **P1**

**formatFindings 3-column output breaks the cold-KV recovery row parser**

This changes the findings table shape from `| Sev | Finding |` to `| Sev | Category | Finding |`. The comment previously above this function (now removed) explicitly noted the row shape was kept in sync on purpose with `parsePriorReview`'s recovery parser in `src/review-state.ts`. That parser is unchanged in this diff and still expects a 2-column row, so a row like `| 🔴 | security | **Title** |` will be misparsed — the category text will bleed into the recovered title, corrupting finding identity used for triage dedup after a cold-KV event.

claims.title: hasP0 readiness check misses P0 findings reported only as inline comments
claims.text:
🟡 **P2**

**hasP0 readiness check misses P0 findings reported only as inline comments**

`hasP0` is computed only from `modelReview.general_findings`, but the readiness score is meant to reflect overall blocking severity. A model can (and per the shared prompt instructions, is expected to) report P0 findings via `inline_comments` when they target a specific line — the prompt explicitly says to prefer inline comments over general findings when a finding has a specific code location. If a P0 is reported only inline, `hasP0` stays false and `computeReadinessScore` can return 3 or 4 (a 'looks fine' readiness bar) even though a critical, non-suppressible P0 exists in the review. This directly undermines the readiness score's stated purpose of flagging P0 presence.

claims.title: priorBotReviews SHA comparison uses metadata SHA but idempotency check compares against context.headSha string form — confirm consistency of SHA formats
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**priorBotReviews SHA comparison uses metadata SHA but idempotency check compares against context.headSha string form — confirm consistency of SHA formats**

parseReviewMetadata's `sha` is whatever was written into `<!-- ai-review:sha=... -->`, which is `context.headSha` (full SHA) per `formatReviewBody`'s `headSha` param. The idempotency check compares `meta.sha === context.headSha` (full SHA), which is consistent. But the external/legacy path still compares against `legacyMarker` built from `context.headSha.slice(0, 12)` (short SHA). This asymmetry (full SHA for new format, short SHA for legacy format) is intentional and appears correct given the two formats, but worth a comment noting why the two paths use different SHA lengths, since it's easy to introduce a bug here in future changes by conflating full vs short SHA comparisons across the two code paths.

claims.title: reviewCount emitted in metadata is one behind the persisted value (unresolved from prior review)
claims.text:
🟡 **P2**

**reviewCount emitted in metadata is one behind the persisted value (unresolved from prior review)**

`reviewCount: (state?.reviewCount ?? 0) + 1` is used when building the metadata block, but `saveReviewState` separately increments `state.reviewCount` again (`(state.reviewCount ?? 0) + 1`) before persisting. Since the value passed into `formatReviewBody` is computed from the *pre-save* `state?.reviewCount`, and the persisted state object built afterward at the bottom of `buildReview` still uses `reviewCount: state?.reviewCount ?? 0` (not incremented) before being passed to `saveReviewState`, the number written into the review body and the number ultimately persisted can diverge across saves. This exact issue was already flagged by Sourcery (Comment 1) and by your own prior review pass — confirming it is still present in this diff.

claims.title: hasP0 correctly checks both general_findings and inline_comments for P0 readiness scoring
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**hasP0 correctly checks both general_findings and inline_comments for P0 readiness scoring**

This correctly checks P0 across both `modelReview.general_findings` and `modelReview.inline_comments`, resolving the previously-flagged gap where inline-only P0 findings would not drag the readiness score to 1. One remaining nuance: this uses `modelReview.inline_comments` (all inline comments from the model) rather than `effectiveInlineComments` or `reviewComments` (the post-filtered/post-dedup set actually posted). If P0 findings are later dropped by suppression, dedup, or anchoring failures, the readiness score would still reflect the original P0 presence even though it's no longer visible in the posted review — arguably correct (readiness reflects underlying risk, not what got posted) but worth confirming this is the intended semantic.
